rationale: Although the article draws on empirical fieldwork concerning arsenic-contaminated rural drinking water in Bangladesh (C1=yes, C3=yes), its analytical focus is feminist cultural/political ecology—specifically how societal, spatial, ecological, and bodily factors and ideological constructs of masculinity and femininity produce gendered subjectivities in everyday practices. No legal, regulatory, administrative, tariff/subsidy, formal tenure/documentation, or utility-structure mechanism is examined (C2 narrow=no; E03 wrong exposure), and gendered subjectivity rather than service access is the primary outcome focus (C4=unclear).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded (E03) because it examines sociocultural gender ideologies, embodied subjectivities, informal norms, and socio-ecological materialities rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure/documentation, tariff, or utility-governance rule. Under the literal/broad Criterion 2 wording, references to 'water management', 'direct resource use/control/access', and 'prevailing norms and practices' could plausibly encompass informal institutional or community governance arrangements, yielding 'unsure'.

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing from fieldwork conducted in Bangladesh on arsenic contamination of drinking water
gendered subjectivities are simultaneously (re)produced by societal, spatial and natural/ecological factors, as well as materialities of the body and of heterogeneous waterscapes.

multiple social and ecological factors interact in complex and interlinked ways to complicate gender-water relations, whereby socio-spatial subjectivities are re/produced in water management and end up reinforcing existing inequities.
